subject: chemistry

concepts.title: Systems and Types of Systems
concepts.definition: The part of the universe chosen for thermodynamic study is called a system; everything else is the surroundings. Systems are classified as open (exchange matter and energy), closed (exchange energy only), and isolated (exchange neither).
concepts.key_idea: The boundary determines whether a system is open, closed, or isolated based on what can cross it.
question_patterns: classify the given system as open closed or isolated
what type of system is a sealed thermos flask
distinguish between open closed and isolated systems with examples
why is the universe considered an isolated system
identify the system type when only energy can be exchanged

solution_steps.explain: Locate the physical or imaginary boundary separating the system from the surroundings.
Determine whether matter, energy, or both can pass across the boundary.
If both matter and energy cross: open; if only energy crosses: closed; if neither crosses: isolated.

worked_examples.question: Classify a cup of hot tea open to air as a thermodynamic system.
worked_examples.solution: The tea can exchange heat with the air and matter (vapour) can escape, so both matter and energy cross the boundary.

worked_examples.question: Classify a sealed rigid steel container holding gas.
worked_examples.solution: The rigid sealed walls prevent matter exchange but heat can still flow through the steel walls.

exercises.question: Classify a thermos flask as a system type and justify.
Give one example each of an open, a closed, and an isolated system.

concepts.title: Surroundings, Work, Heat and Energy
concepts.definition: Surroundings are everything outside the system. Work is energy transfer due to a driving force acting through a distance; heat is energy transfer due to temperature difference; energy is the capacity to do work.
concepts.key_idea: Heat and work are path-dependent modes of energy transfer, not state functions.
question_patterns: state the differences between heat and work
is heat a state function explain
calculate the work done when a gas expands against constant pressure
what is meant by surroundings in thermodynamics
explain why work and heat are path functions

solution_steps.action: identify the mode of energy transfer
solution_steps.explain: Determine whether energy is transferred as heat (temperature difference) or as work (force times distance).
Heat absorbed by system is positive, work done on system is positive; released heat and work done by system are negative.
The change in internal energy equals the sum of heat and work transferred.

worked_examples.question: A system absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on the surroundings. Find the change in internal energy.
worked_examples.solution: q = +500 J (absorbed), w = -200 J (work done by system), so delta_U = q + w = 500 - 200 = 300 J.

worked_examples.question: A gas expands doing 150 J of work while losing 80 J of heat. Calculate delta_U.
worked_examples.solution: q = -80 J (heat lost), w = -150 J (work done by system), delta_U = -80 + (-150) = -230 J.

exercises.question: A system does 250 J of work and absorbs 300 J of heat. Calculate delta_U.
Explain with an example why heat is a path function and not a state function.

concepts.title: Extensive and Intensive Properties, State Functions
concepts.definition: Extensive properties depend on the amount of matter (mass, volume, enthalpy); intensive properties do not (temperature, pressure, density). State functions depend only on the initial and final states, not the path.
concepts.key_idea: A state function is determined solely by the state of the system, making its change independent of the path taken.
question_patterns: classify the given property as extensive or intensive
is enthalpy an extensive or intensive property
which of the following is a state function
explain the difference between state function and path function
give two examples each of intensive and extensive properties

solution_steps.explain: Determine whether the property changes with the quantity of matter in the system.
If the property doubles when the system size doubles, it is extensive; if unchanged, it is intensive.

solution_steps.action: classify as state or path function
solution_steps.explain: If the value depends only on the end states it is a state function (e.g., internal energy); if it depends on the path it is a path function (e.g., heat, work).

worked_examples.question: Classify temperature, mass, and density as extensive or intensive.
worked_examples.solution: Temperature does not change with amount (intensive); mass changes with amount (extensive); density is ratio of two extensive quantities and is intensive.
worked_examples.answer: Temperature: intensive; Mass: extensive; Density: intensive

worked_examples.question: Is internal energy a state function? Justify.
worked_examples.solution: Internal energy depends only on the initial and final states of the system and not on the path, so it is a state function.
worked_examples.answer: Yes, internal energy is a state function

exercises.question: Classify pressure, volume, and molar heat capacity as extensive or intensive.
Explain why heat and work are path functions with a suitable example.

concepts.title: First Law of Thermodynamics (Internal Energy and Enthalpy)
concepts.definition: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed. The change in internal energy equals heat added plus work done on the system. Enthalpy is defined as H = U + PV.
concepts.formula: delta_U = q + w; H = U + PV
concepts.key_idea: The first law is the law of energy conservation applied to thermodynamic systems; enthalpy measures heat content at constant pressure.
question_patterns: state and explain the first law of thermodynamics
calculate delta_U given heat and work values
derive the relation between delta_H and delta_U
what is enthalpy and how is it related to internal energy
calculate delta_H for a reaction at constant pressure

solution_steps.explain: Sum the heat transferred and the work done to obtain the change in internal energy.
For a process at constant pressure, the pressure-volume work term is P times the change in volume.
Enthalpy change equals internal energy change plus the PV work term.

worked_examples.question: A system absorbs 800 J of heat at constant pressure and the volume increases by 2 L against 1 atm. Find delta_U and delta_H (1 L atm = 101.3 J).
worked_examples.solution: w = -P*delta_V = -(1 atm)(2 L) = -2 L atm = -202.6 J. delta_U = q + w = 800 - 202.6 = 597.4 J. At constant pressure delta_H = q = 800 J.

worked_examples.question: For a reaction, delta_U = -50 kJ and delta_n_gas = 1 at 298 K. Calculate delta_H (R = 8.314 J/mol/K).

exercises.question: A system absorbs 600 J of heat and 300 J of work is done on it. Find delta_U.
For a reaction delta_U = -100 kJ and delta_n_gas = 2 at 300 K. Calculate delta_H.
State the first law of thermodynamics and define enthalpy.

concepts.title: Heat Capacity and Specific Heat
concepts.definition: Heat capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a substance by 1 K. Specific heat is the heat capacity per unit mass. Molar heat capacity is per mole.
concepts.formula: q = C * delta_T; C = c * m
concepts.key_idea: Heat capacity relates the heat absorbed or released to the resulting temperature change of the substance.
question_patterns: calculate the heat required to raise the temperature of a substance
find the specific heat given heat mass and temperature change
what is the difference between heat capacity and specific heat
calculate the molar heat capacity of a substance
determine the final temperature after heat is added

solution_steps.action: identify heat capacity and temperature change
solution_steps.explain: Note the heat capacity (or specific heat and mass) and the initial and final temperatures.
If specific heat is given, multiply by mass to get the total heat capacity.
Multiply the heat capacity by the temperature change to obtain the heat absorbed or released.

worked_examples.question: Calculate the heat required to raise the temperature of 500 g of water from 20 C to 80 C (specific heat = 4.18 J/g/K).
A 2 mol sample of a gas has molar heat capacity 29 J/mol/K. Find heat needed to raise temperature by 50 K.

exercises.question: Find the heat needed to raise 250 g of a substance (c = 0.9 J/g/K) by 40 K.
Distinguish between heat capacity and specific heat capacity with units.

concepts.title: Measurement of Delta U and Delta H
concepts.definition: Delta U is measured using a bomb calorimeter at constant volume where delta_U = q_v = C_cal * delta_T. Delta H at constant pressure is delta_H = q_p. The two are related by delta_H = delta_U + delta_n_gas * R * T.
concepts.formula: delta_U = C_cal * delta_T; delta_H = delta_U + delta_n_gas * R * T
concepts.key_idea: Bomb calorimetry gives delta_U at constant volume; enthalpy change at constant pressure is obtained by correcting for the gaseous mole change.
question_patterns: calculate delta_U from bomb calorimeter data
convert delta_U to delta_H using delta n gas
what is a bomb calorimeter used for
derive the relation between delta_H and delta_U
calculate the enthalpy change from calorimetric data

solution_steps.explain: Multiply the calorimeter heat capacity by the observed temperature change.
Count moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants.
Add the PV correction term delta_n_gas * R * T to delta_U.

worked_examples.question: In a bomb calorimeter, combustion of 0.5 mol fuel raises temperature by 4 K (C_cal = 10 kJ/K). Find delta_U per mole.
worked_examples.solution: q_v = C_cal * delta_T = 10 * 4 = 40 kJ for 0.5 mol. Per mole: 40 / 0.5 = 80 kJ/mol. delta_U = -80 kJ/mol (exothermic).

worked_examples.question: For a reaction delta_U = -200 kJ and delta_n_gas = -1 at 298 K. Calculate delta_H.

exercises.question: A bomb calorimeter (C_cal = 8 kJ/K) shows a 5 K rise for 1 mol of substance. Find delta_U.
delta_U = -150 kJ, delta_n_gas = 2, T = 300 K. Calculate delta_H.
Explain why a bomb calorimeter measures delta_U and not delta_H directly.

concepts.title: Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation
concepts.definition: The total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or in several steps, because enthalpy is a state function.
concepts.key_idea: Hess's law allows calculation of unknown enthalpy changes by combining known reactions algebraically.
question_patterns: apply hess law to calculate the enthalpy of a reaction
calculate delta_H using given thermochemical equations
state hess law and give its significance
determine the enthalpy of formation using hess law
combine the given reactions to find the target enthalpy change

solution_steps.explain: Identify the reaction whose enthalpy change is to be found.
Reverse, multiply, or divide the given thermochemical equations so they sum to the target, adjusting their enthalpy values accordingly.
Add up the enthalpy changes of the adjusted steps to get the overall enthalpy change.

worked_examples.question: Given: C(s)+O2(g)->CO2(g) delta_H=-393.5 kJ; CO(g)+1/2O2(g)->CO2(g) delta_H=-283.0 kJ. Find delta_H for C(s)+1/2O2(g)->CO(g).
worked_examples.solution: Reverse the second reaction: CO2(g)->CO(g)+1/2O2(g) delta_H=+283.0 kJ. Add to first: C(s)+O2(g)+CO2(g)->CO2(g)+CO(g)+1/2O2(g). Cancel: C(s)+1/2O2(g)->CO(g). delta_H = -393.5 + 283.0 = -110.5 kJ.

worked_examples.question: Given: N2(g)+2O2(g)->2NO2(g) delta_H=66.4 kJ; N2(g)+O2(g)->2NO(g) delta_H=180.5 kJ. Find delta_H for 2NO(g)+O2(g)->2NO2(g).
worked_examples.solution: Reverse second: 2NO(g)->N2(g)+O2(g) delta_H=-180.5 kJ. Add to first: 2NO(g)+2O2(g)->2NO2(g)+O2(g). Simplify: 2NO(g)+O2(g)->2NO2(g). delta_H = 66.4 + (-180.5) = -114.1 kJ.

exercises.question: Given S(s)+O2(g)->SO2(g) delta_H=-297 kJ and SO2(g)+1/2O2(g)->SO3(g) delta_H=-99 kJ. Find delta_H for S(s)+3/2O2(g)->SO3(g).
State Hess law and explain why it works based on the nature of enthalpy.

concepts.title: Enthalpy of Bond Dissociation, Combustion, Formation and Atomization
concepts.definition: Standard enthalpy of bond dissociation is the heat to break a bond in gaseous state; of combustion is heat released on burning one mole; of formation is heat to form one mole from elements; of atomization is heat to form gaseous atoms from the substance.
concepts.key_idea: Different standard enthalpy changes describe specific chemical and physical transformations under standard conditions.
question_patterns: calculate the enthalpy of reaction using bond enthalpies
define standard enthalpy of combustion with an example
calculate the enthalpy of formation of a compound
what is the enthalpy of atomization
estimate delta_H using average bond enthalpies

solution_steps.explain: Identify all bonds broken in reactants and all bonds formed in products with their bond enthalpies.
Add the bond enthalpies of all new bonds formed in the products.
Reaction enthalpy equals energy to break bonds minus energy released forming bonds.

worked_examples.question: Calculate delta_H for H2(g)+Cl2(g)->2HCl(g). Bond enthalpies: H-H=436, Cl-Cl=242, H-Cl=431 kJ/mol.
worked_examples.solution: Bonds broken: H-H + Cl-Cl = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ. Bonds formed: 2*H-Cl = 2*431 = 862 kJ. delta_H = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ.

worked_examples.question: Estimate delta_H for CH4(g)+2O2(g)->CO2(g)+2H2O(g). Bond enthalpies: C-H=413, O=O=498, C=O=745, O-H=463 kJ/mol.

exercises.question: Calculate delta_H for N2(g)+3H2(g)->2NH3(g). Bond enthalpies: N-N=163, H-H=436, N-H=391 kJ/mol.
Define standard enthalpy of formation and standard enthalpy of combustion with one example each.
What is enthalpy of atomization? Give an example for NaCl(s).

concepts.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics and Entropy
concepts.definition: The second law states that the total entropy of the universe always increases for a spontaneous process. Entropy is a measure of disorder or randomness in a system.
concepts.key_idea: Spontaneous processes proceed in the direction of increasing total entropy of the universe.
question_patterns: state and explain the second law of thermodynamics
calculate the entropy change for a process
predict whether a process is spontaneous from entropy change
what is entropy and how is it related to disorder
calculate delta S for phase transition at constant temperature

solution_steps.explain: For a reversible process at constant temperature, entropy change equals heat transferred divided by temperature.
The surroundings absorb or release heat equal and opposite to the system at the surroundings temperature.
If the total entropy change of the universe is positive the process is spontaneous; if negative it is non-spontaneous.

worked_examples.question: Calculate delta_S when 1 mol of water vaporizes at 100 C. delta_H_vap = 40.7 kJ/mol.
A system absorbs 500 J at 300 K reversibly. The surroundings are at 300 K. Find delta_S_universe.
worked_examples.solution: delta_S_system = 500/300 = 1.67 J/K. delta_S_surroundings = -500/300 = -1.67 J/K. delta_S_universe = 1.67 - 1.67 = 0 (reversible).

exercises.question: Calculate delta_S for melting 2 mol of ice at 0 C (delta_H_fus = 6.0 kJ/mol).
State the second law of thermodynamics and define entropy.
Explain why the entropy of the universe increases in a spontaneous process.

concepts.title: Gibbs Energy Change and Spontaneity; Third Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.definition: Gibbs energy G = H - TS predicts spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure: delta_G < 0 is spontaneous, delta_G > 0 is non-spontaneous, delta_G = 0 is at equilibrium. The third law states the entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is zero.
concepts.key_idea: Gibbs energy combines enthalpy and entropy into a single criterion for spontaneity; the third law provides an absolute reference for entropy.
question_patterns: calculate delta_G and predict spontaneity
determine whether a reaction is spontaneous at a given temperature
state the third law of thermodynamics
find the temperature at which a reaction becomes spontaneous
explain the relationship between delta_G delta_H and delta_S

solution_steps.explain: Obtain the enthalpy and entropy changes for the process from tabulated data or given values.
Subtract the product of temperature and entropy change from the enthalpy change.
Negative delta_G means spontaneous, positive means non-spontaneous, zero means equilibrium. The temperature at which delta_G = 0 is T = delta_H / delta_S.

worked_examples.question: For a reaction delta_H = -50 kJ and delta_S = -100 J/K at 300 K. Is it spontaneous?
worked_examples.solution: delta_G = delta_H - T*delta_S = -50000 - 300*(-100) = -50000 + 30000 = -20000 J = -20 kJ. Since delta_G < 0, spontaneous.

worked_examples.question: A reaction has delta_H = 40 kJ and delta_S = 120 J/K. Find the temperature above which it becomes spontaneous.
worked_examples.solution: Set delta_G = 0: T = delta_H / delta_S = 40000 / 120 = 333.3 K. Above 333.3 K, delta_G becomes negative.

exercises.question: delta_H = -90 kJ, delta_S = -0.2 kJ/K, T = 400 K. Calculate delta_G and predict spontaneity.
State the third law of thermodynamics and explain its significance for absolute entropy.
Explain how Gibbs energy serves as a criterion for spontaneity at constant T and P.
